progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: chem-m7-c04a (hydration of ethene: equation, steam, phosphoric acid, about 300 °C, high pressure, two gas molecules to one; conditions on the arrow; the conditions card), chem-m7-c04b (substitution as a swap, two products; haloalkanes made from alkanes with UV light), chem-m7-c05 (ethanol; naming and classifying alcohols; the polar O–H bond; ethanol boils at 78 °C; the ethanol bottle plate), chem-m7-c01 (naming), Module 5: chem-m5-c02 (reversible reactions reach equilibrium; the ⇌ arrow), chem-m5-c04 (pressure and gas molecules; a catalyst speeds both directions and does not shift the position), chem-m5-c03 (temperature and exothermic reactions; recommended prerequisite). Year 11: balancing equations; ionic compounds such as NaBr; limewater turns milky with carbon dioxide; distillation separates liquids by boiling point. Year 11 or Biology: enzymes are biological catalysts damaged by high temperature; respiration with and without oxygen (one clause, with a plain meaning). Not assumed: fermentation, reflux, aqueous (given a plain meaning), feedstock (given a plain meaning), single-pass recycling.
progression.startsWith: Compare hydration, substitution and fermentation starting materials. The video opens: This bottle holds ethanol. It could have started as sugar, fermented by yeast. It could have started as ethene, a gas made from crude oil or natural gas.
progression.stopsAfter: writing the equation and conditions for each of the three routes; explaining the equilibrium arrow, the pressure, the catalyst, the temperature compromise and recycling in hydration; explaining why hydroxide substitutes a haloalkane and why it is heated under reflux; explaining each fermentation condition and the limewater result; explaining why each product must be separated and how; judging the routes by feedstock, conditions, rate and separation. No combustion, no elimination, no mechanism names.
progression.nextLesson: burning ethanol and alcohols as fuels (route chem-m7-c07, "What does burning an alcohol tell us about fuel choice?").

teaching.task: The ethanol in this bottle could have started as ethene from crude oil or natural gas, as a haloalkane in a flask, or as sugar fermented by yeast. How can we make ethanol, and how do the conditions and the separation help us judge each route?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) one product, three starting materials; choose by starting material, conditions and separation (1); (2) hydration recalled: reversible, so ⇌; two gas molecules become one, so pressure favours ethanol (2); (3) the catalyst speeds both directions; lower temperature would give more ethanol but too slowly (3); (4) little reacts per pass, so cool, condense, recycle ethene, distil the ethanol from water; the plant runs nonstop, so fast and continuous, but from crude oil or natural gas (4); (5) bromine leaves its carbon slightly positive, so hydroxide is attracted, bonds, and bromide leaves: substitution (5); (6) heat speeds it, reflux keeps the volatile liquids, distil the product; the OH lands where the halogen was, so a chosen alcohol can be made (6); (7) glucose to two ethanol and two CO₂, balanced; yeast's enzymes are the catalyst, on the arrow (7); (8) warm for the enzymes, air out so less sugar is respired aerobically and more goes to ethanol, gas out so pressure cannot build; limewater shows CO₂ (8); (9) ethanol poisons the yeast at about 15%, so filter and distil; the vapour is richer in ethanol because it boils lower (9); (10) each route wins on something different, so the judgement depends on feedstock, energy and purity needed (10); memory aid (11); two attempts and brief feedback (12 to 15); handoff (16); key notes (17).
teaching.conversationalApproach: the ethanol in one bottle could have started as sugar, as ethene from crude oil or natural gas, or as a haloalkane in a flask, so the video asks how we can make ethanol and how each route's starting material, conditions and separation decide which to choose. Hydration of ethene with steam returns from the addition video as an equilibrium with two half arrows, where high pressure favours one gas molecule from two, the catalyst speeds both directions without moving the equilibrium, and about 300 degrees is a rate against yield compromise. Only a few per cent reacts per pass, so the mixture is cooled, unreacted ethene is recycled and the ethanol distilled, a fast continuous process from a non-renewable feedstock. Substitution swaps the bromine of bromoethane for an OH from aqueous hydroxide, because the bromine leaves its carbon slightly positive for the hydroxide ion to attack; reflux keeps the volatile liquids in the flask while heating speeds it up, and the OH lands where the halogen was. Fermentation is balanced atom by atom with yeast on the arrow as the catalyst, and the school setup gives each condition its reason (about 35 degrees, air kept out, gas let out, limewater turning milky), stopping near 15 per cent so the mixture is distilled. The routes are judged feature by feature with no single winner, and the memory aid is yeast, warm, no air. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: This bottle holds ethanol. It could have started as sugar, fermented by yeast. It could have started as ethene, a gas made from crude oil or natural gas. Or, in a lab, it could come from a haloalkane, like bromoethane, heated in a flask. Same molecule every time. So how can we make ethanol, and which way would you choose? That depends on what you start with, the conditions each route needs, and how you get the ethanol out at the end.
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) "A student keeps two flasks of glucose solution and yeast at 35 °C. Flask A is fitted with a bung and delivery tube. Air is bubbled through flask B the whole time. After two days, flask B contains less ethanol than flask A. Explain this difference, and write a balanced equation for the fermentation of glucose." New framing (Revision 2: a controlled comparison that really occurs; the scenes show flask A's setup; the one changed condition is the cause to find); the shared temperature rules out warmth as the cause. Crossed mistake: "C₆H₁₂O₆ + yeast → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂" (yeast written as a reactant; the marker-reported mistake in 2021 Q25, a non-consumed substance written as a reactant, `../research/question-types-chem-m7.md`). (A2) "1-Bromobutane is heated under reflux with aqueous sodium hydroxide. Write a balanced equation for the reaction, name the organic product, and explain why the mixture is heated under reflux." New haloalkane (the scenes use bromoethane and 2-bromopropane; the site uses 1-chloropropane); tests the swap on the same carbon, the salt, c05 naming and the reason for reflux. Crossed mistake: "butan-2-ol" (the OH moved to another carbon; the site MC Q1 distractor pattern).
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "investigate the production of alcohols, including:; substitution reactions of halogenated organic compounds; fermentation" Hydration of ethene is not listed under this dotpoint (it is `C7-IQ3-01`, chem-m7-c04a); it is recalled here as the third route because the route start compares all three starting materials. this video starts by comparing the starting materials of three routes to ethanol (ethene from crude oil or natural gas, a haloalkane, and glucose from plants), and stops at judging each route's conditions and how the ethanol is separated. It teaches: hydration recalled from chem-m7-c04a (ethene and steam, phosphoric acid catalyst, about 300 °C, about 60 to 70 atmospheres); the reaction is reversible, so it is written with an equilibrium arrow (chem-m5-c02 callback); at 300 °C all three substances are gases, two gas molecules become one, so high pressure favours ethanol (chem-m5-c04 callback); the catalyst speeds both directions and does not move the equilibrium (chem-m5-c04 callback); the forward reaction releases heat, so 300 °C is a compromise between yield and rate (one sentence; Module 5 temperature callback, see Open decisions); only a few percent of the ethene reacts per pass, so the mixture is cooled, ethanol and water condense, and unreacted ethene is recycled; the ethanol is then distilled from the water; substitution: a haloalkane heated with aqueous sodium hydroxide gives an alcohol and a sodium halide (bromoethane to ethanol and NaBr), because the halogen leaves the carbon slightly positive and the negative hydroxide ion is attracted to it; the OH takes the halogen's place on the same carbon (2-bromopropane gives propan-2-ol), so the route can make a chosen alcohol; heating under reflux speeds the reaction without losing the volatile haloalkane and alcohol, because the upright condenser returns their vapours; the alcohol is then distilled from the mixture; fermentation: glucose to ethanol and carbon dioxide, balanced, with yeast on the arrow because its enzymes are the catalyst; the school setup as a short apparatus sequence (glucose solution and yeast in a flask, a warm water bath at about 35 °C, a bung and delivery tube that keep air out and let carbon dioxide escape, limewater turning milky); why each condition (enzymes work fastest when warm and are damaged when too hot; with oxygen, yeast can respire some sugar aerobically to carbon dioxide and water, so less ethanol forms; gas must escape so pressure cannot build); fermentation usually stops at about 15% ethanol, so the yeast is filtered off and the mixture distilled, the vapour richer in ethanol because ethanol boils at 78 °C and water at 100 °C (fractional distillation in industry, one clause); judging the routes by feedstock (renewable or not), conditions and energy, rate (continuous or batch) and separation, with no single best route. Not here: the four alkene additions and their conditions in full (chem-m7-c04a; recalled once with the conditions card); naming and classifying alcohols, boiling points (chem-m7-c05); burning ethanol, combustion equations and enthalpy, biofuel energy data (chem-m7-c07; the site's L11 figures are not used); elimination with ethanolic hydroxide (screen chip only; chem-m7-c08 and c13); the substitution mechanism by name (SN1, SN2) and leaving-group order (site card 2 feature 3; author note e); Markovnikov's rule; starch hydrolysis by amylase (site, author note h); breadmaking and carbonation (site Insight); country case studies (Brazil, Germany; correction 8); the 95.6% azeotrope (author note i).

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. Colour key as chem-m7-c04a, c04b and c05: carbon skeleton ink; hydrogens soft grey; oxygen brick red, the OH ringed red; the C=C teal; bromine deep orange-brown; condition chips navy on the arrow; the equilibrium arrow navy with two half heads; the second product boxed in thin grey ("+ NaBr", "+ 2CO₂"). Board layout (constant): top-left the short task chip ("Route 1: hydration", "Route 2: substitution", "Route 3: fermentation"); centre the equation stage strip, one equation at a time; plates small at the left or right (larger only in scenes 8 and 9, where the apparatus is the content); the route board returns small at the top in scenes 10 and 16. Clutter rule: at most three text items bright at once; every label fades when its sentence ends; the previous equation or plate leaves before the next one draws. Reuse: painted plates (inspected 22 Oct): `m7-ethanol-fuel-bottle-v1.png` (an amber glass bottle with a glass stopper, pale liquid, no label; 2000 × 2000; hook and handoff, coded label "ethanol"); `m7-crude-oil-barrel-v1.png` (a plain dark steel drum, no label; 2000 × 2000; hook and scene 4, coded label "crude oil → ethene"); `m7-reflux-apparatus-v1.png` (a round-bottom flask of pale orange liquid on a heating mantle, an upright water-jacketed condenser clamped to a retort stand, red and blue water hoses; no people; 2000 × 2000; scene 6 and feedback 2); `m7-school-distillation-setup-v1.png` (a flask on a heating mantle, a still head with a thermometer, a sloping water-jacketed condenser with hoses on its own stand, a conical collecting flask; no people; 2000 × 2000; scenes 4 (small, silent) and 9). All small, scale uniformly only, never stretched. Considered, not used: `m6-limewater-clear-v1.png` and `m6-limewater-milky-v1.png` (inspected: a limewater tube in a wooden rack with a bent delivery tube entering from the upper left; a separate flask plate could not be joined to that tube reliably, so the limewater tube is drawn inside the new setup plates in the same style); `m6-conical-flask-v1.png` (inspected: an empty conical flask; no bung, tube or contents); `g1-sugar-bowl-v1.png` (inspected: a bowl of table sugar with a spoon; sucrose, not the glucose solution in the equation); `m6-red-wine-glass-v1.png` (inspected: a glass of red wine; drink context not needed). New plates: `m7-fermentation-setup-start-v1.png` and `m7-fermentation-setup-bubbling-v1.png` (hook, scene 8, feedback 1); see Assets. No human figures.
